```typescript
type AcademyContentBlock =
  | { type: 'heading'; content: string; level?: 2 | 3 }
  | { type: 'paragraph'; content: string }
  | { type: 'code'; content: string; language?: string }
  | { type: 'callout'; content: string; variant?: 'info' | 'warning' | 'tip' }
  | { type: 'table'; headers: string[]; rows: string[][] }
  | { type: 'link-card'; title: string; url: string; description: string; source?: string }
  | { type: 'tool-card'; name: string; category: string; description: string; url?: string; features?: string[] }
```

---

**Section 9: How This Was Built**

This is the meta case study — documenting how Vibe Voyager itself was built using Claude Code with agent teams. This is living proof of everything the game teaches.

Cover:
1. **Overview** — Vibe Voyager was built entirely with Claude Code (Opus 4.6) using subagent-driven development. 9 phases, 39 tasks, up to 13 parallel agents.
2. **The Stack** — Next.js 15, TypeScript, React 19, Tailwind CSS v4, Motion, HTML5 Canvas, Howler.js, localStorage
3. **Timeline** — Built in approximately 1 week (starting 2026-03-07)
4. **Build Phases:**
   - Phase 1: Scaffolding (2 sequential agents)
   - Phase 2: Core Infrastructure (4 parallel agents, 1,835 lines)
   - Phase 3: Core Screens (5 parallel agents, ~1,461 lines)
   - Phase 4: Game Systems (3 parallel agents, ~1,561 lines)
   - Phase 5: Mini-Games (5 parallel agents, ~1,718 lines)
   - Phase 6: Planet Content (8 parallel agents)
   - Phase 7: Academy Content (5 parallel agents)
   - Phase 8: Polish (4 parallel agents)
   - Phase 9: Deployment
5. **Agent Team Architecture** — How subagent-driven development works: fresh agent per task, zero file conflicts via careful task decomposition, main thread handles git commits
6. **Tools Used** — Skills: brainstorming, writing-plans, subagent-driven-development, executing-plans. Plugins: superpowers, compound-engineering, context7. Agents: Explore, code-reviewer, code-architect
7. **Key Decisions** — Why Next.js over a game engine (agents parallelize React better), why localStorage over a backend (no auth needed for a teaching tool), why Tailwind v4 (CSS-first config)
8. **Metrics** — Total lines of code: ~10,000+. Total agent invocations: 30+. Zero type errors across all parallel agent work.

Use tables for phase data, callouts for key insights, paragraphs for narrative.
Include a callout (variant: 'tip'): "This entire website is an exercise in agentic development — built by the same practices it teaches."

---

**Section 10: Career Paths**

Cover 4 career paths that the game's skills map to:

1. **AI-Native Developer** — Uses AI tools daily for coding, testing, and review. The evolution of the traditional developer.
   - Key skills: prompt engineering, AI code review, tool selection, quality assurance
   - Game stats mapping: High Vibe, moderate Architecture
   - Tools: Cursor/Windsurf, Claude Code, CodeRabbit
   - Salary range context: Growing demand, traditional developer salaries + AI premium

2. **AI Full-Stack Developer** — Builds full-stack applications with AI assistance. Masters both the AI tools and the underlying technology.
   - Key skills: frontend/backend architecture, agent integration, MCP setup, deployment
   - Game stats mapping: Balanced all stats
   - Tools: Next.js + AI IDEs, MCP servers, deployment automation
   - Entry path: Traditional dev + AI upskilling

3. **Prompt Engineer** — Specializes in crafting effective prompts and system instructions. The bridge between human intent and AI capability.
   - Key skills: prompt design, evaluation, system instructions, few-shot examples
   - Game stats mapping: High Vibe, high Protocol
   - Tools: Claude API, evaluation frameworks
   - Note: Role is evolving — increasingly merged with AI engineering

4. **Agentic Engineer** — Designs and orchestrates multi-agent systems. The fleet commander.
   - Key skills: agent architecture, MCP/A2A protocols, orchestration, security (HITL)
   - Game stats mapping: High Architecture, high Command
   - Tools: Agent SDKs, MCP, A2A, LangGraph/CrewAI
   - This is the frontier — highest demand, fewest practitioners

Include:
- Heading and intro about the changing landscape
- Tool-cards for each career path (category = career path type)
- A comparison table: headers ["Role", "Core Skills", "Game Stats", "Demand Level"]
- Callout (variant: 'info') about skills remaining relevant regardless of role
- Callout (variant: 'tip') about the T-shaped developer — deep in one area, broad across all
- A concluding paragraph about continuous learning

**Guidelines:**
- Do NOT use \! in any strings (causes TS1127)
- Section 9 should feel like a real case study — detailed, data-driven, inspiring
- Section 10 should help students map game experience to real career choices
- 20-30 content blocks per section
